summary:
Santander operates under Colombia's national framework, which is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the route under which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition with no surgical requirement. Marriage equality has been available since 2016, adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025. A comprehensive trans law was still before the legislature in 2025.

The courts have also intervened in detention: a Colombian court ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.

Enforcement lags the statute badly. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025, and one report counted 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025 alone. A separate count put 41 trans people killed in 2023 and eight between February and April 2024. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, welcoming the government's legal reforms while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected and that widespread discrimination and violence must be addressed urgently as killings rise.

Where armed groups operate, the threat is organised rather than incidental. In Caquetá, three armed men told trans woman Tatiana Cespedes, 51, she had one week to leave town or be killed; she hid for a week and fled at night. "Social cleansing" flyers circulated on streets and by WhatsApp in that department named "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets, a campaign run by armed groups still operating despite the 2016 peace agreement. In Guajira, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". Trans women in Caquetá reported few options beyond sex work, and discrimination confines trans women nationally largely to hairdressing or sex work.

Targeted killings also continue in ordinary urban settings. Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in Bello, Antioquia in April 2025; the assault was filmed, the video went viral from 5 April, and she died the following afternoon. Police interrogated local residents but no one was arrested. President Gustavo Petro ordered an urgent investigation and solidarity events were held in several cities. Her mother Sandra Borja stated, "They killed her for being who she was". The article placing her death also recalls earlier fatal attacks on LGBT people, including a trans rough-sleeper stabbed while sleeping.

Some of this violence has been prosecuted as an international crime rather than ordinary homicide. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against them constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity. The UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern.
tangentialFactors:
None of the incidents in the sources took place in Santander, and the department is used here only as one point on a national pattern. The Millerey killing occurred in Bello, Antioquia; the armed-group campaigns were documented in Caquetá and Guajira. The distinction matters for a visitor because the same national legal text applies in Santander while the specific pressures differ: in Caquetá and Guajira the threat comes from armed groups issuing lists and deadlines, whereas the Antioquia case shows lethal violence in an ordinary urban setting with bystanders filming and no arrest following.

The national totals quoted across the sources are inconsistent in scope and period. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders over January to May 2025; a separate count put 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025; 41 trans people were killed in 2023 and eight between February and April 2024. These are not contradictory so much as differently defined and differently timed, and none of them isolates Santander.

Colombia's framework compares favourably with neighbouring jurisdictions on paper: no surgical requirement, notary-based marker change, marriage and adoption rights, and explicit trans and non-binary identity markers. The comparison holds only at the level of statute, since the UN Independent Expert's May 2025 findings describe institutional progress and lived experience as disconnected across the country.

Colombian residents change the sex marker on their identification by signing a document before a notary, a route open since June 2015 and grounded in Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 recognising self-recognition without any surgical or psychiatric prerequisite.

Residents have access to marriage equality since 2016 and to adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and national identity documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025. A comprehensive trans law remained under legislative consideration in 2025, so protections still rest substantially on constitutional and court rulings rather than a single statute.

Trans detainees have judicially protected rights in the prison system following a court ruling on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty. Residents facing threats from armed groups are the population most exposed: trans women in Caquetá reported few livelihoods beyond hairdressing or sex work, and the economic narrowing compounds the physical risk.

Crimes against LGBT people have been charged as war crimes and crimes against humanity before the Special Jurisdiction for Peace, with the state accepting that conflict-driven violence against them amounts to gender persecution.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Santander-specific law, enforcement practice, detention case or documented incident against trans people is available from the sources consulted; the department's position is inferred from the national framework and from incidents recorded elsewhere in Colombia. Santander-specific homicide, discrimination and police-response data were not sourced.

Whether notary offices in Santander are applying the June 2015 marker-change procedure as written, and whether the "trans" and "non-binary" markers issued from November 2025 are being produced without friction at local providers, remains unresolved in the sources.

Whether the comprehensive trans law under consideration in 2025 has since been enacted, stalled or amended is unresolved here. The sources date to 2024 and 2025 and no later legislative status was available.

Statistics on trans killings are reported by different bodies over different periods, and none of them isolates Santander or any comparable-sized department; the counts cannot be reconciled into a single rate on this record.
